items.literal_solution: The result contains three rows: A=1, A=2 and A=NULL. The subquery is empty; NOT IN is true for every left operand, including NULL.
items.difficulty_reason: One direct application of SQLite’s empty-set NOT IN rule. The B>0 filter does not create another substantive decision because S is explicitly empty.
items.distractors_reason: The alternatives distinguish excluding the NULL left value, keeping only it, and treating an empty right set as rejecting every row; these reflect membership/NULL misconceptions.
items.relevance_reason: Directly practices the requested interaction between membership predicates, NULL and an empty subquery.
items.premise_reason: The stated rows, column names and exact query determine the result under the specified SQLite context; no added case facts are needed.

per_choice.reason: Incomplete: the NULL row also passes NOT IN against the empty subquery.
Exactly the three returned values; all three left operands satisfy NOT IN against the empty set.
Incomplete: the ordinary values 1 and 2 pass as well.
Incorrect: the empty subquery makes NOT IN true, so all three rows pass.

sqlite_execution.ddl: CREATE TABLE T(A); INSERT INTO T VALUES (1), (2), (NULL); CREATE TABLE S(B);

queries.sql: SELECT A FROM T WHERE A NOT IN (SELECT B FROM S WHERE B>0)

items.literal_solution: Neither A row has an ON match. In particular, NULL=NULL is not true. LEFT JOIN produces one NULL-extended B row per A row, and both satisfy B.Y IS NULL. The output values are 1 and NULL.
items.difficulty_reason: Requires connected inferences: distinguish ordinary equality from IS NULL, determine that both left rows lack an ON match, then apply WHERE to the NULL-extended rows. This is meaningful application of interacting NULL and outer-join semantics.
items.distractors_reason: The single-value and empty-result alternatives can arise from dropping a NULL left value, confusing original B NULL rows with joined NULL extension, or treating LEFT JOIN like an inner join.
items.relevance_reason: Directly exercises the stated difficulty predicting LEFT JOIN results with NULL comparisons and post-join filtering.
items.premise_reason: The stated rows, column names and exact query determine the result under the specified SQLite context; no added case facts are needed.

per_choice.reason: Incomplete: the NULL-valued A row is preserved by LEFT JOIN and also passes B.Y IS NULL.
Incomplete: A.X=1 has no B match and its NULL-extended B.Y also passes the filter.
Exactly the output: both unmatched A rows survive the IS NULL filter.
Incorrect: LEFT JOIN preserves each unmatched A row, and their NULL-extended B.Y values satisfy IS NULL.

queries.sql: SELECT A.X FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.X=B.Y WHERE B.Y IS NULL

items.difficulty_reason: A simple filter leaves only one row, so the apparent DISTINCT-versus-GROUP BY comparison has no surviving duplicates to analyze. The extra query syntax does not make this level 3.
items.distractors_reason: All distractors require either creating a second 2 that does not exist or discarding the only qualifying row without any relevant condition. They are distinct but weak alternatives for the stated basic-SELECT learner.

items.literal_solution: For P.K=5, Q has the qualifying row (5,1), so EXISTS is true. For P.K=10, no Q row has matching K, so EXISTS is false. The result is one row containing 5.
items.difficulty_reason: A familiar correlated-EXISTS membership check: identify the sole positive matching row. The NULL-valued Q row does not alter the existence of (5,1), so there is no harder competing NULL or duplicate effect to resolve.
items.distractors_reason: Both keys can result from ignoring correlation; 10 alone from reversing EXISTS; no rows from allowing the NULL-valued candidate to invalidate the independently qualifying row.
items.relevance_reason: Directly practices a correlated EXISTS predicate and identifies which outer row has a qualifying inner row.
items.premise_reason: The stated rows, column names and exact query determine the result under the specified SQLite context; no added case facts are needed.

per_choice.reason: Exactly correct: only K=5 has a matching Q row whose M is greater than zero.
Incorrect: K=10 has no Q match and therefore fails EXISTS.
Incorrect: K=10 fails EXISTS, while K=5 passes.
Incorrect: Q row (5,1) satisfies both predicates for P.K=5.

sqlite_execution.ddl: CREATE TABLE P(K); INSERT INTO P VALUES (5), (10); CREATE TABLE Q(K, M); INSERT INTO Q VALUES (5, NULL), (5, 1);

queries.sql: SELECT P.K FROM P WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Q WHERE Q.K=P.K AND Q.M>0)

items.literal_solution: LEFT JOIN produces (10,NULL) and (20,'a'). The WHERE condition R.X='a' rejects (10,NULL), because the comparison is NULL, and keeps (20,'a'). The output is one row (20,'a').
items.difficulty_reason: Requires carrying the unmatched left row through the join and then recognizing that a right-side WHERE predicate removes it. These linked decisions apply the ON-versus-WHERE distinction to an actual result, rather than merely recalling that LEFT JOIN retains left rows.
items.distractors_reason: Keeping both rows reflects ignoring the post-join filter; keeping the unmatched row alone confuses selection polarity; no rows reflects losing the valid equality match or mishandling NULL.
items.relevance_reason: Directly exercises the requested LEFT JOIN and right-side filtering interaction.
